title: Reserve Fund, Insurance and a Plan B When Borrowing to Buy a Home
desc: How big a reserve fund a home loan needs, whether to buy loan insurance, and what to do if you cannot repay. A Plan B helps keep your home if income falls.
summary: How to build a reserve fund, consider insurance and prepare a Plan B when borrowing to buy a home, so the family does not fall into overdue debt or have its property enforced.
body: p

Borrowing to buy a home is a commitment of 15–25 years. In that time, job loss, illness, young children or rising interest rates can all happen. Preparing a financial “cushion” in advance helps the family get through hard periods without losing the home.
h2
1. What happens if you cannot repay?
p

When you borrow to buy a house, the house is usually the mortgaged asset (Article 317 of the Civil Code). If you fail to repay when due or repay improperly, the lender has the right to enforce the secured asset (Article 299). In addition, overdue debt bears higher interest – for example, for a social housing loan from the Vietnam Bank for Social Policies, overdue interest is 130% of the lending rate (Decree 261/2025/ND-CP, amending Clause 4, Article 48 of Decree 100/2024/ND-CP). So a reserve fund matters as much as your own equity contribution.
h2
2. How big should the reserve fund be?
p
A prudent rule: keep a separate sum equal to at least 6 months of loan repayments plus essential living costs, not to be used for buying the house or furniture.
p

An assumed example: borrowing VND 1.2 billion over 20 years, assuming 10% interest per year → repayments of about VND 11.58 million per month. A reserve fund for the repayments alone for 6 months is about VND 69.5 million. If essential spending adds VND 10 million per month, the fund should be about VND 130 million.
p
This means: if you have VND 300 million, do not put it all into your equity contribution – plan the savings portion first.
h2
3. Should you buy insurance when borrowing?
ul
Many loans come with a suggestion to buy insurance (life, health, property). Ask clearly whether the insurance is compulsory to get the loan or only voluntary.
Read the benefits carefully: in which cases it pays out, whether it pays the bank in place of the borrower, waiting periods and exclusions.
Compare the insurance cost with the benefits; prioritise protecting the family's main earner.
Fire and explosion insurance on the house protects the very asset that is mortgaged.
h2
4. Plan B when income falls
ol
Contact the bank early, before the loan becomes overdue: ask about restructuring the repayment term, rescheduling the debt or reducing the amount paid each period (depending on the bank's policy).
Cut non-essential spending; use the reserve fund to keep to the repayment schedule.
Create extra income from the house: rent out a room or a floor – make a clear lease contract.
Borrow from relatives with a loan note stating the amount and term clearly; the agreed interest must not exceed 20% per year (Article 468 of the Civil Code).
Sell proactively when there is no other way: selling while you can still control the price is usually better than letting the asset be enforced.
h2
5. Early repayment: pros and cons
p

When you have surplus money (a bonus, the sale of other assets), paying down principal reduces interest and risk. However, under Clause 2, Article 470 of the Civil Code, for a term loan with interest repaid early, all the interest for the agreed term must be paid, unless otherwise agreed or provided by another law. Bank loan contracts usually set a separate early-repayment fee – read it carefully and work out whether it is worthwhile. Do not use up the whole reserve fund on early repayment.
h2
6. Checklist
ul
You have a reserve fund of at least 6 months of repayments, held separately.
You have calculated repayments at an interest rate 3% per year higher than the preferential rate.
You know the early-repayment fee and overdue interest in the contract.
You understand the accompanying insurance (compulsory or voluntary, benefits).
The whole family knows about the loan and the Plan B.
note

This article is for reference only and is not financial advice. The figures in the example use an assumed interest rate. Debt restructuring policies, insurance and early-repayment fees are set by each bank and insurer – consider your ability to repay and ask carefully before signing.
